references.text: God gives similar promises to Isaac to be with him and bless him, with the same assurance of divine presence.
God reminds Jacob of His promise and encourages him to return to his homeland, assuring him that He will be with him.
God confirms His promise to Jacob regarding the land and descendants after his return to Canaan, as a fulfillment of the promise of restoration.
God promises Jacob to go down with him to Egypt and bring him back up again—a parallel promise of presence and restoration.
God's promise to Moses to be with him is a parallel assurance of divine presence at a crucial mission.
Moses assures Israel that God will go before them, not let them go, and not forsake them—the same type of promise concerning presence and faithfulness.
God's promise to Joshua: 'I will not let you go and I will not forsake you'—a direct parallel to the promise not to forsake Jacob.
Jesus' promise to be with His disciples all days until the end of the world is a New Testament parallel to God's promise of enduring presence.
The author quotes the promise 'I will never let you go and never forsake you' as an eternal assurance of God's faithful presence.
Both verses emphasize God's active role in preserving and rebuilding His people in the promised land.
Theological parallel: The promise to be present everywhere is confirmed in 1 Chronicles as a historical reality for David.
Theological parallel: The promise to be present everywhere is confirmed in 2 Samuel as a historical reality for David.
Direct linguistic and theological connection: The promise not to forsake is given from Jacob to all the people of Israel in Deuteronomy.
